MUNICIPAL COURT.
A Girl Drugged and Assaulted—A Friendly Quarrel—Several Drunks.
At the Municipal Court this morning
A Girl Drugged and 'Assaulted—A Friendly Quarrel—Several Drunks.

At the Municipal Court this morning Charles Clark was charged with disorderly conduct on Saturday night and assaulting Officer Brown on his way to the station after being arrested, He was fined $5 and costs. Frank Rogers, formerly a waiter in the Ebbit House, was charged with drunkenness. He said he was working at present in Newark and came to visit friends in this city on Saturday, when he got drunk. He was discharged. Hugh Doyle, white, and Theodore Washington, colored, were charged with trespass, by riding on the steam cars without a ticket Saturday night. Each was fined $5 and costs.

Millie Thomas, a pretty looking girl of 16, was charged with being found lying intoxicated on Third street, near Monroe, Sunday morning at 1 o'clock. The officer said there was no doubt that the girl was drugged by some men who assaulted her and then threw her over the fence. Her grandmother, with whom she lived, was respectable. Her parents lived at Greenbank. Judge Ball tried to elicit some information from her as to her company, but she would give no account of herself. She was fined $1 and costs. John McIntire, drunk, $1 and costs.

Michael Lynch was charged with fighting and chewing the ear of a man named John Lucy last evening. John Lucy, who had part of his ear bitten off, said it was a friendly quarrel. He knew nothing as to how the quarrel originated, as both had been drinking. Lynch was discharged on paying the costs. Thomas Callan, drunk, $2 and costs.

In the case of Chris. Brooks, colored, charged with stealing chickens, City Sollicitor Lynam asked that the case be postponed for one week. He said that in making the arrest Officer Sherer was obliged to use his revolver, inflicting a wound on the prisoner's leg. He wished to have him removed to the almshouse to have the wound, which is a slight one, attended to. The postponement was granted.

City Sollicitor Lynam asked the court to hold a boy named Henry Roddell in bonds as a witness against several other boys who were charged with theft, robbery and miscellaneous offenses. He said Roddell had given information against these boys, and he wanted a postpone-ment for one week. Roddell was held in $200 ball to appear on next Monday morning.

greensboro-greensboro-1890-08.A2:
THE LATEST NEWS
FROM NORTH CAROLINA.
A fire occurred at Burlington Thursday. One store and the postoffice were burned.
Down at Greensboro a day or ago negroes were whipped by a policeman, properly delegated, for fighting.
Rev. Sam P. Jones will commence meetings at Winston on the 25th of September. The meetings will continue not less than ten days.
Judge Bynum, of Charlotte, sold a large portion of his land to Mr. Sink, of Winston, this week. Considerations, fifteen thousand dollars.
At Greensboro several valuable horses have died this season with lockjaw, which seems to have become almost epidemic among the livery stables there.
Considerable interest is shown at High Point over the rediscovery of a fine mineral spring about two miles from town. It had been filled up for years.
A little boy of twelve named Willie Medlin killed himself drinking whiskey near Youngsville, Wakecounty, Monday. He was begged to take a drink by a middle aged man.
Prof. and Mrs. W. F. Fentress, principals of one of the leading schools in Guilford county, have both been extremely
—Congressman W. H. H. Cowles is at his home in Wilkesboro, and is in very feeble health. His physicians says he should have been at home long ago, but he stood steadily at his post to vote against the election bill.

—There is an organized movement within the Alliance to defeat Senator Vance, and that, too, in spite of the fact that there are many good and true democrat Alliancemen who are hostile to the movement.—Charlotte Chronicle.

—Messrs. Duke, of Durham, have begun the erection of a mammoth storage warehouse in connection with their factory at Durham. The structure will be five stories high, one of the highest in the State, and the dimensions will be 200x60 feet.

—Greensboro is said to have still another paper. John C. Tipton, who has been editor of the Patriot, daily and weekly, since its revival in January, retired from that paper on Monday, and will begin the publication of the Guilford Democrat about August 20. The Democrat will be an orthodox paper.
We have been shown the throttle to Mr. John Smyre's engine, which Superintendent McBee has kindly had enclosed in a handsome case with a glass front and presented to Mrs. Smyers. It was taken from the engine in which he was killed in the fearful accident on Saluda mountain in June.—Newton Enterprise.

The report that a successor to Superintendent Dixon of the Orphan Asylum had been appointed. Superintendent Dixon has not even tendered his resignation! The appointment of a successor when made will be made by the directors—and the directors have not even yet been called together.—Raleigh News and Observer.

Thos. Camp, of Rutherford county, N. C., had ten sons and one daughter by his first wife. He married again as his second wife, Miss Margaret Carney, of North Carolina, and had by her ten sons and two daughters. Then he died. The twenty-three children of Thos. Camp were, as might have been expected, a prolific and stalwart race. Only one of them, a daughter, approached the father's record, however. She had twenty-two children. At a reunion a few years ago in Douglass county, Ga., fully 3,000 descendents were present. A day or two ago, at the residence of the late Major William A. Camp, near Dalton, Ga., assembled all of his seven sons and their descendants in a family reunion, the occasion being their mother' seventieth birthday.

—Essie Skeen, 4 years old, of Charlotte, and a goat, of nowhere especially, were playing on the edge of the Carolina Central's deep cut Saturday. The goat was staked, like a cow in a pasture. All at once both rolled down into the railroad cut. The rope which was fastened to the goat's neck caught on a fence post. On the loose end was a loop, which caught around Essie's neck and drew tight. Both the child and the goat were suspended by their necks fully six feet from the bottom of the cut. Another child gave an alarm and Essie and the goat were rescued. The child was black in the face and totally unconscious. Dr. Wilder, by the use of ammonia, and forcing air in her lungs, finally restored her to consciousness. She is now all right. Of course the goat did not mind a little thing like that.

A Brute in Human Shape.
sheriff of Ray county, Tenn., left here this morning with Henderson Fox, a negro, whom he is taking back to answer a charge of rape. The negro was arrested in the Indian Territory a few days ago by Heck Thomas and brought to this city for safe keeping. The crime committed by the brute was a most heinous one, his victim being a twelve-year-old white girl afflicted with the pitiable misfortune of blindness. Lincoln 20, Nebraska City 10. NEBRASKA CITY, Neb., August 17.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—The home team played with the Lincoln association team today. The game was quite exciting after the first inning, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by a score of 20 to 10. Batteries-For Lincoln, Clare and McFarland; for Nebraska City, Hensel, Mohler and Wilson. Umpire—Turner. People's Party at Valentine.
VALENTINE, Neb., August 17.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—The people's party met in mass convention yesterday and nominated a commissioner, coroner and county attorney; also elected ten delegates to the representative convention for Keya Paha and Cherry counties. Delegates are practically instructed for T. G. Black, a labor nominee, for representative.

Wood River Items.

Wood River, Neb., August 17.—[Special to THE BEE.]—During a thunder storm here last night lightning struck the livery barn of Williams & White and killed one horse. No other damage was done, although the barn was filled with horses.

The Catholics held a picnic here yesterday, which was largely attended.

Improvements at Blue Hill.

Blue Hill, Neb., August 15.—[Special to THE BEE.]—Blue Hill is one of the liveliest towns in the state. On every hand are springing up buildings of all kinds, substantial evidences of a prosperous future.

Swift Justice to a Black Brute.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., August 17,—Henderson Fox, the negro who outraged Miss Annie Dowling, was lynched at Trenton tonight by a mob of about two hundred men from the neighborhood where the crime was committed. The sheriff and jailer did all in their power to prevent the mob's getting at the prisoner, and summoned a large guard, which surrounded the jail. The mob was determined, however, and ran over the guard and demanded the keys of the jailer. He was compelled to give them up. The prisoner was taken out and hanged to a tree.

A Laborer Killed.

CHEYENNE, Wyo., August 17.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—John Breen, a laborer working on the Cheyenne & Northern, was killed yesterday by being thrown from a work train, falling under the wheels. Breen was thirty years old and his family resides at Pacific, Mo.

Hanged Herself at Seventy.

HUNTINGTON, Ind., August 17.—One of the oldest residents of this county, Mrs. Sarah Hunt, aged seventy years, living at Andrews, six miles west of this city, committed suicide by hanging this morning. The only cause assigned for the deed is continued ill health.

NEWS OF THE WEEK.
Latest Intelligence from All Parts of the World.
A double tragedy was enacted at St. Louis. Edward Hake shot and killed his young wife and then inflicted a mortal wound on himself.

When a train of refrigerator cars arrived at New York from Chicago, pounding was heard proceeding from one of them. Upon its being opened, four tramps jumped out. They boarded the car at Chicago and had nothing to eat since but ice and a limited supply of provisions. They were nearly frozen.

A fire at the Mount Athos Monastery, Belgrade, Turkey, destroyed several of the buildings. Twelve monks were killed.

Bruce Huffman, Bert Dickinson and John Reynolds were caught in the act of setting fire to August Maxe's building, Clinton, Ia. All were arrested next day, and Dickinson and Huffman were held to appear before the grand jury, their bail being fixed at $1,000 each.

Edward Happy, a green cow-puncher, was lost in a snow storm in Wyoming last February. The remains of horse and rider were found by a hunter recently twenty miles from the road. Happy's body was in a faid state of preservation, and will be shipped to his old home in Ohio.

The statue of Lafayette, presented by France to the United States, has arrived at New York.

Ransom Shivers, of Tennille, Ga., a wealthy planter, and leader in the alliance party, was driving, when his horses became frightened at an approaching train, and ran away. Mr. Shivers was thrown out of his wagon and hurled head foremost against a tree. He died instantly, his neck having been broken.

William Dennis, the engineer, and Columbus Maggard, a young helper, were killed instantly at an explosion of a boiler at the new gas works in Lincoln, Neb. Nobody was around at the time of the accident except the two men.

Miss Alsbaugh, of Upper Sandusky, O., a pretty and heretofore universally respected girl of nineteen, eloped with a colored fellow named Hart, a comparative stranger, who was a cook at one of the hotels. Parents and friends of the young lady are crazed at her action.

Clinton Schueck, who shot himself in the head five weeks ago, after murdering Louisa, the 14-year-old daughter of William Brunst, at Swamp, Pa., died in his cell in the county prison. Soon after the discovery of the murder Schueck was found hidden and rather than face the angry crowd shot himself in the eye and ear.

Adolph Shade, a German bookkeeper of Chicago, in getting off a grip car was thrown violently to the ground. He was picked up in an unconscious condition and taken to his home, where he died.

A tornado and hail storm in the Department of Aube, France, ravaged eighteen communes, destroying the harvested and growing crops. The loss is estimated at nearly 25,000,000 francs.

Henderson Fax, a negro who attacked Miss Annie Dowling, a beautiful young white girl, near Trenton, Tenn., last May, was taken from jail and lynched by a mob of 200 men.

Samuel Jacobson, a prominent business man of San Francisco, was shot through the breast and probably wounded fatally by footpads. He was stopped by two men just as he was about to enter his house, and ordered to throw up his hands; but before he could obey the order one of the men fired, the bullet passing almost through Jacobson's body.

Mrs. Ellen McLane, of Chicago, has been keeping a lamp burning in her room all night. Recently the lamp exploded. Several pieces struck Mrs. McLane, who was lying in bed, inflicting painful injuries. She will probably die.

A shark came to grief in New London Conn., at the hands of Annie Babcock, a Quonochontaug maid. The monster became fool-hardy, and on the crest of a mighty surf billow came away up the strand where Annie was strolling and was clubbed to death by her.

Joseph Addison Jameson, senior partner of the banking house of Jameson, Smith & Co., New York, committed suicide at his Fifth avenue residence by hanging himself with a sheet from the door of his bed-room.

By the falling of a scaffold which had been erected on a building on the Nevski Prospect, St. Petersburg, Russia, eight persons were killed and eight injured.

Miss Maggie Jenson was struck by a North Side cable train in Chicago, and sustained severe internal injuries.

Tom Woodward, a negro, charged with highway robbery, was taken from the jail at Humboldt, Tenn., by a masked mob and lynched.

Three employees were injured in a collision between a freight and a coal train on a side track at Midway, twenty miles west of Pittsburg on the Pennsylvania railroad. Trains were delayed several hours.

The Crystal flour mills at Minneapolis were burned with several small frame dwellings and sheds near by. The mills were valued at $40,000.

William Ryan, an aged laborer who was run over by a hose cart, at Lake View, Chicago, died at the German hospital.

Charles Nelson, thirty years old and unmarried, was killed in Chicago by a Santa Fe engine.

A four-year-old son of Martin Van Every, a Buffalo druggist, at his clothes a-fire while playing with matches and was burned to death.

NEWS SUMMARY.
Nearly all the mills at Fall River, Mass., have closed down.

The Minnesota crops will be larger this year than ever before.

Emperor William's visit to England was not a great popular success.

Henderson Fox, a negro ravisher, was lynched by a mob at Trenton, Tenn.

Twenty-six persons were killed by the falling of a tenement house at Berlin.

England and France have agreed on a division of disputed African territory.

The Fort Wayne and the Findlay and Western railroads have been consolidated.

Near Arkansas City, Ark., a negro was lynched for attempted assault on two girls.

The Italian government has forbidden any further emigration to South America.

The discovery of a large cave with prehistoric remains in it is reported from Kansas City.

A young man was attacked by eight sharks while wading and narrowly escaped with his life.

A colonist sleeping car on the Great Northern railway was burned with all its contents at Ada, Minn.

A call has been issued for the prohibition state convention to be held in Des Moines, September 4.

Secretary Windom has made an explanation of the retention of trade dollars in the treasury vaults.

Negotiations are in progress to construct a tunnel under the bay between Staten Island and Bay Ridge.

The report comes of another appearance of the sea serpent on the Eastern coast. This time it was dead.

The Western Passenger Association contract, which expires September 1, will probably not be renewed.

The panic among the christian inhabitants of Armenia is spreading and hundreds are fleeing to Persia.

Colorado banks have been heavily swindled by a man passing as a representative of the Nicaragua Canal.

Eugene Harrison, a young man of Evansville, Ind., was soundly cowhided by a Mrs. Taylor, whose daughter he had insulted.

Dr. J. E. Chesholm, charged with the murder of Sheriff Stone of Lafayette county, Arkansas, has been released on bail.

The election in the Chickasaw nation passed off quietly, resulting in a victory for the Nationals and the reelection of Gov. Byrd.

Five hundred machinists of Pittsburg, Pa., struck for nine hours as a day's work. Nearly all the shops have granted the demand.

By the breaking of a scaffold on a new building in St. Petersburg, Russia, Saturday eight workmen were killed and eight injured.

Sixty thousand persons attended the mass meeting in Buenos Ayres to rejoice over the fall of President Celman of the Argentine Republic.

Henry M. Stanley has surprised Frenchmen by expressing the opinion that Ribot made a good bargain in the Anglo-French agreement.

The Italian government has sent to the powers the draft for a proposal for a convention to establish an international maritime service on the Red sea.

A dispatch from Buenos Ayres states that a bill will be introduced in congress authorizing the government to lease 250,000,000 acres of national land.

Arthur Day, in jail at Rochester, N. Y., for bigamy, is proved to have killed his first wife at Niagara Falls. His own sister informed the police of his deed.

Census Superintendent Porter estimates the population of the country at 64,000,000. He expects to have the counting finished by the end of this month.

A natural gas well was struck three miles from Santa Barbara, Cal. It is said to be one of the largest in America. The estimated flow is 3,000,000 feet per day.

Chauncey Depew, president of the New York Central, in an interview was asked his opinion on the situation of affairs in regard to the strike on that road. Depew in reply said he did not think it was necessary to express an opinion, in view of the fact that the strike was ended.

john-brown-anderson-1890-08-05.A1:
A Rape Flend Lynched.
Special to the Gazette.

NAVASOTA, TEX., Aug. 4.—A report reached here from Anderson of the hanging of a negro, John Brown, charged with committing rape on a white girl in this county. He was confined in the Houston jail for safe-keeping and was taken back to Anderson last night, and secreted by the sheriff. His hiding place was discovered there, and about 3:50 p. m. to-day citizens took him out and hanged him and filled his carcass with bullets. The negro confessed his guilt before he died.
john-brown-anderson-1890-08-05.A2:
THE ANDERSON LYNCHING.
The Negro Made a Confession Before He was Strung up—Courthouse Mass Meeting. Correspondence of the Gazette.
The Negro Made a Confession Before He was Strung up—Courthouse Mass Meeting. Correspondence of the Gazette.

ANDERSON, TEX., Aug. 4.—John Brown, colored, who raped a white girl near Iola was brought from the Houston jail early Monday morning and held in a private house by Sheriff Scott. A crowd of 500 citizens demanded the prisoner of Scott. He refused to give him up, when a search was commenced and he was soon found and brought out and carried two miles from town and hung by at least 2000 of our people. He said he was guilty and ought to die. He said to the reporter that he had been watching an opportunity to catch the young lady about three weeks. The young girl is well connected and of good family. The people after the hanging went to their homes.

District court adjourned for the term.

County court continued all cases until the fall term on account of so much excitement.

To-day is ond of the happiest days of old Anderson. At least 1500 people were here demanding that justice be done them. Anderson gained the courthouse by a handsome majority. Several speeches were made denouncing men who would run negroes from other counties to vote in our contest. W. B. Montgomery, F. G. Dunn and W. M. McNew of Montgomery county were here and received a vote of thanks by the people for trying to keep negroes from Montgomery county from voting in our county.
john-brown-anderson-1890-08-05.A4:
TEXAS STATE NEWS.
SELECTED FROM OUR EXCHANGES AND STATE SPECIALS.
Galveston has had a heavy rain storm.

Joe Sayers is renominated by acclamation in the Tenth congressional district.

The stone of the new college for colored people will be laid today at Sherman.

Uvalde has shipped about 175,-000 pounds of honey this year, at 8 cents per pound.

Prof. O'Brien is exhibiting at Sunset, some muggets of gold bearing rock found in Montague county.

Freight Conductor Gilkey, of the Texas and Pacific, lost $1,500 by the Toyah fire.

The Fort Worth Union Bethel mission, which was organized a short time ago, is doing good work.

The Corpus Christi board of trade have invited ex-President and Mrs. Cleveland to come and look at the future seaport of Texas when they come south.

Stella Kuchler, an orphan girl 10 year old, has received criminal treatment at the hand of a Mexican and his mistress at Fort Worth.

Several people are ill and one lady has died of a very peculiar disease at Waco, which the doctors are calling chicken pox.

John Brown, a negro, is strung up by the citizens of Navasota for rape of a white girl, which crime he confessed.

C. P. Kean, a sheepman, is shot and killed by James Boyen. They were alone on the prairies. Boyen surrendered himself.

J. S. Tensley, for forgery gets five years at Montague. Tom Higgins, cow theft two years. Three men each charged with murderous assaults get $25 fine each.

Engineer Davis, who had charge of the engine which ran over and killed two girls, who jumped from a Galveston street car, some time back, is completely exonerated from all blame.

A 12-year-old boy jumped off a Texas and Pacific train, near the Dallas fair grounds and had his left leg so crushed that amputation was necessary. His right leg was also broken.

Mrs. Adelaine Prince, of Galveston, is playing Celia in "As You Like It," with Ada Rehan's company in London, and has received very high praise.

In a difficulty over a crop of corn made by a farmer named Smith on Farmer Bowman's place at Decatur, the former was shot in the hand.

Lawrence, the 10-year-old son of J. M. Davis, of Sherman, accidentally shot himself by drawing a winchester from the back part of a hack to the front front seat. He lived about 30 minutes, and his only suffering seemed to be for his mother, when the news should reach her.

Rev. Mr. Erwin, of Ennis, while removing some cattle from an enclosure, was charged upon by a vicious bull. A young lady, Miss Emma Mullin, ran to assistance, struck the bull in the face till he was blind, which enabled her to put up some of the bars and check the beast, until he could be caught and fastened.

Taken From Jail and Lynched. HUMBOLDT, TENN., Aug. 18.—About midnight on Saturday a mob took a negro, named Thomas Woodward, from jail here and hanged him. Woodward was one of three negroes who assaulted and robbed J. A. Greer last Thursday night. DRAFTING POPULAR. BARRILLAS TAKES THIS MEANS TO INCREASE GUATEMALA'S ARMY. Attracted to Public Entertainments and Then Seized-All Who Kefuse Are Shot-Americans Are Safe.
SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 18.—The Central American mail recently brought letters from George W. Cool, formerly a well-known physician of this city, but who has been in Guatemala during the past year. Dr. Cool says a proclamation has been issued that all men who were not ready for military duty would be shot. Nearly all the men who first went to the front have been killed in battles with Salvadorians.

"If Ezeta marches to the city," the letter says, "he will probably sack the town. The Americans are safe, for they receive protection at the Legation. Every servant, even those on the coffee plantations, have been drafted into the war, and there are not enough left to supply food. Provisions bring enormous prices. Business is at a standstill and the city is under martial law. Twenty Americans and as many Germans and Frenchmen offered their services to Barrillias, but they were refused. About 25,000 soldiers have already left the city for the frontier. "Men are attracted to public entertainments and are then seized by the police and drafted in the army."

Three employees were injured in a collision between a freight and a coal train on a side track at Midway, twenty miles west of Pittsburg on the Pennsylvania railroad. Trains were delayed several hours.

The Crystal flour mills at Minneapolis were burned with several small frame dwellings and sheds near by. The mills were valued at $40,000.

William Ryan, an aged laborer who was run over by a hose cart, at Lake View, Chicago, died at the German hospital.

Charles Nelson, thirty years old and unmarried, was killed in Chicago by a Santa Fe engine.

A four-year-old son of Martin Van Every, a Buffalo druggist, at his clothes a-fire while playing with matches and was burned to death.

Read THE PLAINDEALER ABOUT PERSONS AND THINGS.
W. G. Louthal, of Newstead, Ky., has been appointed State Superintendent of the Afro-American Farmers' Alliance of Kentucky.

James Bragg, a prominent Afro-American politician and chairman of the Republican Central Council of Mobile, Ala., died at his residence August 18.

Mrs. Myla Powell, a North Carolina ex-slave died at South Bend, Ind., August 16th, aged 106 years. She retained her mental faculties, mind and hearing to the last.

Robert R. Walterman, a barber of St. Paul, committed suicide by firing two shots into his anatomy last Sunday. Meloncholy is supposed to have induced the deed.

Thomas Woodward was taken from the jail at Humboldt, Tenn., August 13 by a mob of white men and hanged to a tree. Woodward was guilty of assault and robbery.

The work of an Afro-American census taker of Nashville, Tenn., was so complete that although two men were sent out by the government to verify his report, no omissions could be found in his territory.

J. E. Rankin, president of Howard University, Washington, D. C., has a thoughtful paper on "The Ethical Training of Afro-American Youth" in the August number of "Our Day." Joseph Cook's magazine.

Frank Morris, a married man residing in Youngstown, O., eloped to Pittsburg with his wife's niece, Miss Sadie Lewis, where he secured a license and was married. Mrs Lewis No. 1 merely says "he cannot live in Youngstown again."

Ed. Morrison, a laborer at Carter's camp near Athens, Ga., shot and killed his employer, Henry Hunter, because he discharged him. Morrison who escaped, is being pursued and if caught will be dealt with after the usual Southern method.

George Early and Bird Woods, two of four men convicted of the burning of the village of Rocky Mount, on the night of October 9, 1889, were hanged at that place August 22. Both men were active Republicans and died protesting their innocence.

A large number of the citizens of Hartford, Conn., gave a reception in honor of Mr. Bolding Bowser, the newly appointed Consul to Sierra Leone last Wednesday. After the banquet and speaks Mr. Bowser was presented with a gold headed cane as a souvenir of his old friends.

Mississippi Republicans at a recent meeting passed resolutions asking the Hon. James Hill, who made the race for Congress at the last election in the third Mississippi district to again submit his name as the standard bearer of the Republicans of the Third Congretsional district for a seat in the Fifty-second Congress.

Mr. H. C. Smith, a Democratic lawyer of Birmingham, Ala., who charged Prof. J. G. Clayton principal of the States school with teaching the children Republican doctrines, was publicly denounced at a citizens' meeting held to endorse Mr. Clayton, whose high character has won for him the respect of the community.

David Johnson, a porter on the Northwestern railroad, who sought to follow in the foot steps of the illustrious Solomon came to grief when he took unto himself wife No. 3. He undertook to chastise her when she reproved him for deceiving her, but she retaliated by having him arrested as soon as she was able to move around.

J. J. Montgomery, the only Afro American delegate to the Democratic constitutional convention in session at Jackson, Miss., was seated Wednesday on a vote of 79 to 28. Montgomery is a full blooded Negro, 45 years of age and presented his case in a speech of thirty minutes, which was followed by applause, a compliment paid no other speaker.

G. H. Smith, grocer, cigar and shoe merchant of Durham, N. C., visited Petersburg, Va., last week, to replenish his stock of cigars. He called at a cigar manufactory and the proprietor thinking that he merely intended making some trifling purchase curtly refused to show his goods, thus losing a big sale, as Smith went elsewhere to buy his stock.

The Ninth Baltimore Colored Ohio National Guard, comprising the entire Afro-American Militia of Ohio, is in camp at Washington, C. H. O. In a dress parade which they gave last week, their work was the subject of much flattering comment, and it is said that should they be called on to do service for the State at any time, they will show themselves to be brave soldiers.

John Henderson, who murdered Gilbert Satterwhite, a prominent farmer near Midway, Ky., last week was taken from jail two days later by a mob and hanged to a tree. An accessory to the murder had been arrested, and has no doubt by this time been hung. The men killed Satterwhite because of their discharge from a threshing machine gang a few days ago. The murderer's friends are highly incensed at the hanging.

Editor R. Wright is likely to get the Augusta, Ga., Post-office.

All the colored members of the Louisiana legislature sustained the Lottery bill. Shame!

A Negro in La, at his death willed $5,000 to a white man.

Mr. William Gilbert, the philanthropist and milionaire, left $40 000 in his will for the Gilbert School for Colored Girls in Winstead, La.

Hon. Alexander Clark, of Iowa, has been appointed Minister to Liberia, and his appointment seems to give general satisfaction. — Florida Sentinal.

Miss Mary V. Robinson, of Louisville, Ky., surprised all of her friends by reporting that she had been married to a white drummer from Milwaukee for over one year.

Brother Albert, a Benedict Monk, the only one of color in the United States, was in attendance at the colored Catholic congress. He is well educated a fine speaker and a sociable gentleman.

Thomas Woodward was taken from the jail at Humboldt, Tenn., August 16 by a mob of white men and hanged to a tree. Woodward was guilty of assault and robbery.

Negro Burglar and Murderer.
August 7 Will
Negro Burglar and Murderer.
MONTGOMERY, ALA., August 7.—Will Johnson, a negro boy, burglarized two houses in Opelika yesterday and to-day killed P. J. Moore a merchant of Gold Hill, who was trying to arrest him. A special to the Advertiser says threats of lynching are made.
will-johnson-opelika-1890-08-07.A2:
Killed by a Burglar.
MONTGOMERY, Ala., Aug. 8.—A negro boy named Will Johnson, who had robbed two houses in Opelika, killed P. J. Moore, a merchant, who was endeavoring to arrest him. Johnson was captured, and there are threats of lynching.
will-johnson-opelika-1890-08-07.A6:
STARTED OUT TO BE A DESPERADO Johnson is Only 14, but they're Already Talking of Lynching Him.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., Aug. 8.—John Johnson, a negro boy, 14 years old, was caught robbing the house of Mrs. McClellan at Opelika yesterday. A young white man named Green attempted to capture the boy, and was shot and slightly wounded. The negro ran and took refuge in an empty box car. A watchman named Ingram tried to arrest him there. The boy jumped out and shot Ingram in the breast, inflicting a wound which may prove fatal. Then a man named Stringfellow gave chase to the boy and overtook him, only to receive a shot in the head, which inflicted a dangerous and probably fatal wound.

Johnson got out of the town and reached Gold Hill, seven miles away. In the meantime the officers had telegraphed his description ahead and asked for his arrest. At Gold Hill Jenkins Moore, a Justice of the Peace and the leading merchant of the town, saw the boy walking along the railroad and attempted to arrest him. John again drew his pistol and shot Moore through the heart, killing him instantly. A crowd then started after the boy. He fired several shots at them without effect, and was finally run down and captured after he had discharged all of his cartridges. He was taken back to Opelika and looked up. He confessed that he had killed a white man some time ago, and had started out to be a train robber and desperado. It is feared he will be lynched. A mob threatened the jail last night, but was overawed by the guard provided by the Sheriff.

PRECOCIOUS AND DEPRAVED.
An Alabama Colored Boy a Burglar and Murderer at Fourteen.
The little town of Opelima, Ala., is wild with excitement and a lynching is expected there. Thursday John Johnson, a colored boy fourteen years old, was caught robbing the house of Mrs. McClelland. A young white man named Green attempted to capture the boy and was shot and slightly wounded. The colored boy fled and took refuge in an empty box car. A watchman named Ingram tried to arrest him there. The boy jumped out and shot Ingram in the breast, inflicting a wound which may prove fatal. Then a man named Stringfellow gave chase to the boy and overtook him, only to receive a shot in the head, which inflicted a dangerous and probably fatal wound. Johnson got out of town and reached Gold Hill, seven miles away.

In the meantime the officers had telegraphed his description ahead and asked for his arrest. At Gold Hill, Jenkins Moore, justice of the peace and leading merchant of the town, attempted to arrest him. Johnson drew his pistol and shot Moore through the heart. The crowds of white men then started after the boy, and he fired several shots at them without effect, and was finally run down and captured after he had discharged all of his cartridges. He was taken back to Opelius and lodged in jail. A mob was organized to lynch the boy, but the sheriff had placed a strong guard around the jail and the mob made no attack.
will-johnson-opelika-1890-08-07.A10:
An Alabama Negro Who Has Shot Six People and Killed Three of Them.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., Aug. 9.—Fears are entertained that Joe Johnson, a negro at Opelika, in the eastern part of the State, will be lynched some time to-night. Johnson's crime is that of shooting six people, assaulting a respectable white woman and killing a justice of the peace. He entered the house of Mrs. McClellan for the double purpose of assaulting and burglarizing. The lady's screams brought a young man to her rescue. Johnson turned and fired upon the young man and then fled. A posse started in pursuit immediately.

Later in the day the negro was discovered, by a railroad watchman named Ingram, hiding in a freight car, and upon being ordered out fired on the watchman, wounding him seriously. Yesterday afternoon Johnson was seen near Gold Hill, a station on the Columbus & Western road. Jenkins Moore, a justice of the peace and a prominent merchant of Gold Hill, attempted to arrest him. Johnson drew his pistol and shot Moore through the heart, killing him instantly. A track-walker, named Stringfellow, who had witnessed the murder, grabbed the murderer. In the scuffle that followed Stringfellow was shot through the forehead.

Johnson was arrested, however, and taken to Opelika and lodged in jail. A strong guard was placed around the jail, as Sheriff McGraw had heard that an attempt would be made to lynch Johnson. There is a large crowd outside the jail intent upon lynching the prisoner. Johnson also shot and killed two white men a short time ago.

A Juvenile Colored Desperado.
A Juvenile Colored Desperado. John Johnson, a negro boy fourteen years old, was arrested at Opelika, Ala., the other day, where he is wanted for a dozen crimes. He is charged with murder, highway robbery, burglary, grand larceny and various smaller offenses. The boy had been a fugitive from justice some time, and was captured while in the act of robbing a private residence.
